Bringing Value Models Back: Generative Critics for Value Modeling in LLM Reinforcement Learning

Zikang Shan ††thanks: Work done at Microsoft Research Asia; Email to <shanzikang@stu.pku.edu.cn>; †Correspondence to Li Zhao <lizo@microsoft.com>, Han Zhong <hanzhong@stu.pku.edu.cn> and Liwei Wang <wanglw@cis.pku.edu.cn>. Affiliation: Peking University Affiliation: Microsoft Research Asia    Han Zhong    Liwei Wang    Li Zhao
Abstract

Credit assignment is a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Classical actor-critic methods address this challenge through fine-grained advantage estimation based on a learned value function. However, learned value models are often avoided in modern large language model (LLM) RL because conventional discriminative critics are difficult to train reliably. We revisit value modeling and argue that this difficulty is partly due to limited expressiveness. In particular, representation complexity theory suggests that value functions can be hard to approximate under the one-shot prediction paradigm used by existing value models, and our scaling experiments show that such critics do not improve reliably with scale. Motivated by this observation, we propose Generative Actor-Critic (GenAC), which replaces one-shot scalar value prediction with a generative critic that performs chain-of-thought reasoning before producing a value estimate. We further introduce In-Context Conditioning, which helps the critic remain calibrated to the current actor throughout training. GenAC improves value approximation, ranking reliability, and out-of-distribution generalization, and these gains translate into stronger downstream RL performance than both value-based and value-free baselines. Overall, our results suggest that stronger value modeling is a promising direction for improving credit assignment in LLM reinforcement learning.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a cornerstone of large language model (LLM) post-training, transforming next-token predictors into capable assistants that solve complex problems (Jaech et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025a; Team et al., 2025). Initially popularized through human value alignment (Ouyang et al., 2022; Rafailov et al., 2023), RL is now widely deployed to enhance mathematical reasoning (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025a), code generation (Le et al., 2022), and agentic systems (Team et al., 2025). As these applications demand longer-horizon reasoning and more complex interactions, the ability of the underlying RL algorithms to provide effective training signals becomes a critical bottleneck.

A central challenge in RL is credit assignment: determining which decisions within a long sequence contributed to an eventual outcome (Sutton et al., 1998). This challenge is particularly pronounced in LLM post-training, where supervision is typically limited to a single scalar reward at the end of an entire sequence. Actor-critic methods (Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999) address credit assignment by learning a value function that converts sparse outcome rewards into dense, token-level advantages, providing more informative training signals for the policy. Among these methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) provide a practical and influential instantiation of this idea, combining stable clipped-surrogate optimization with fine-grained advantage estimation via Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) (Schulman et al., 2015). This value-based recipe has been proven effective in various applications including LLM alignment (Ouyang et al., 2022).

Yet in recent practice, PPO-style methods have fallen out of favor. Training an accurate value model at LLM scale is both difficult and computationally expensive, pushing practitioners toward simpler value-free alternatives. Methods such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024) and REINFORCE Leave-One-Out (RLOO) (Ahmadian et al., 2024) bypass the critic entirely by estimating uniform advantages from multiple sampled trajectories, and have gained wide popularity as a practical workaround that achieves competitive performance.

However, this simplicity comes at the cost of precise credit assignment. Without a value function, these methods assign uniform credit across all tokens in a trajectory, effectively reducing sequential generation to a contextual bandit problem (Langford and Zhang, 2007). This over-simplification could cap the performance ceiling of LLM post-training, and the issue grows as the field increasingly targets longer context applications such as complex reasoning, multi-turn conversations and agentic systems. This motivates us to revisit value modeling in LLM RL. Rather than viewing the recent shift toward value-free methods as evidence that critics are unnecessary, we ask: can value models be made accurate and robust enough to restore fine-grained credit assignment in practice?

Our primary contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We analyze the limitations of standard discriminative critics in LLM RL from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Drawing on representation complexity theory, we provide evidence that their difficulty arises in part from limited expressiveness under the one-shot scalar prediction paradigm, rather than from optimization challenges alone. Controlled scaling experiments confirm that their approximation error does not improve reliably with model size and is highly sensitive to random seeds.

  2. 2.

    We propose Generative Actor-Critic (GenAC), which replaces one-shot scalar value prediction with a generative critic that performs explicit chain-of-thought reasoning before producing value estimates, directly addressing the expressiveness limitation above. We further introduce In-Context Conditioning, a mechanism that keeps the critic calibrated to the current policy throughout training.

  3. 3.

    On mathematical reasoning benchmarks, GenAC achieves superior sample efficiency and continues to improve in training regimes where baselines plateau. Supporting analyses show that the generative critic ranks candidate actions more reliably, generalizes better out-of-distribution, and produces interpretable credit assignments that are consistent with reasoning quality.

2 Related Works

Value-Based Algorithms. Although crucial for fine-grained advantage estimation, value modeling remains underexplored beyond standard PPO in LLM RL. VC-PPO (Yuan et al., 2025b) mitigates initialization bias and reward decay through value pretraining and setting λ=1\lambda=1 in TD(λ\lambda) for value learning. We adopt these techniques, but find them insufficient for effective value learning. VRPO (Zhu et al., 2025) introduces a complex information bottleneck architecture to handle noisy supervision; SAE (Gong et al., 2026) formulates a segment-level MDP to apply PPO on. However, all these works rely on discriminative architecture and do not isolate performance gains in value function approximation. Meanwhile, several works propose better ways of utilizing learned value models for effective policy learning (Yue et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a). These works are orthogonal to ours as they do not improve value modeling.

Value-Free Algorithms. Bandit-like algorithms such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) and RLOO (Ahmadian et al., 2024) have gained popularity due to their simplicity and efficiency. While these methods avoid the cost of value modeling, they risk over-simplification and could lower the possible gains of post-training. To obtain fine-grained feedback without value models, methods like VinePPO (Kazemnejad et al., 2025) and SPO (Guo et al., 2025c) use multiple continuous rollouts for unbiased segment-level value estimation. However, these sample-based estimations incur a great inference cost during training. GiGPO (Feng et al., 2025) estimates advantage by utilizing repeated states that exist only in multi-turn agent training rather than general LLM RL.

Fine-Grained Reward Signals. Another line of work tackles credit assignment by augmenting sparse outcome rewards with dense, intermediate reward signals. Process Reward Models (PRMs) (Lightman et al., 2023) provide reward at every intermediate reasoning step, requiring expensive process labels annotated by humans or rollouts (Wang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2024). Subsequent work (Zhong et al., 2025a; Zhong et al., 2025b; Yuan et al., 2025a; Cui et al., 2025) proposes implicit PRMs that require only outcome labels to train. However, both explicit and implicit PRMs are static evaluators highly susceptible to reward hacking and often struggle to generalize. Other approaches design heuristic reward bonuses (Qu et al., 2025). These works reformulate the RL objective with external rewards, while our work focuses on utilizing internal feedback through value estimates.

Generative Reward Models. There is a growing interest in utilizing generative architectures for reward modeling. Early methods (Zhang et al., 2024; Mahan et al., 2024) finetune language models to generate chain-of-thought reasoning before extracting probabilities from indicator tokens, while more recent works (Liu et al., 2025b; Chen et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025b) train models with RL to directly output verbalized rewards. Similar ideas are also explored in PRMs (Zhao et al., 2026; Khalifa et al., 2025; Zha et al., 2025). However, these works are limited to static reward modeling, while we tackle the problem of value modeling, which is inherently more difficult for two reasons: First, reward modeling strictly reduces to value modeling since the terminal value equals the outcome reward. Second, value models are required to be deeply coupled with the active policy that evolves over training. Our generative architecture ensures that the value model remains aware of the capabilities of the evaluated policy, enabling dynamic and accurate value estimation throughout the RL process.

3 Preliminaries

Language Generation as an MDP. Language generation can be modeled as a Markov Decision Process (𝒮,𝒜,P,R,ρ,T)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,R,\rho,T), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the action space, PP is the transition dynamics, RR is the reward function, ρ\rho is the distribution of initial states, and TT is the maximum number of decision steps. At step tt, the state s=x∘y<t∈𝒮s=x\circ y_{<t}\in\mathcal{S} is the concatenation of the prompt xx and the response generated so far y<t=y1∘y2∘⋯∘yt−1y_{<t}=y_{1}\circ y_{2}\circ\cdots\circ y_{t-1}; the action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} is the new generation at granularity of token, segment or response; the transition dynamics PP is deterministic, appending the new generation to the state to obtain the next state st+1=P⁡(st,at)=st∘ats_{t+1}=P(s_{t},a_{t})=s_{t}\circ a_{t}; the reward function RR assigns 00 to all steps except the last, where it provides a binary reward depending on the correctness of the generation. A parameterized policy πθ​(a|s)\pi_{\theta}(a|s) determines the probability of taking action aa at state ss. Its value function V⁡(s)V(s) is defined by the expected cumulative reward if starting at state ss then following π\pi. Its Q function Q⁡(s,a)Q(s,a) is defined by the expected cumulative reward if starting at state ss, taking action aa, then following π\pi. The advantage function A⁡(s,a)A(s,a), defined by Q⁡(s,a)−V⁡(s)Q(s,a)-V(s), depicts the expected improvement in cumulative reward from taking action aa over the average action at state ss, then following π\pi.

Proximal Policy Optimization. PPO and its variants are the most widely used RL algorithm in LLMs. It is efficient through minibatch update and stable by optimizing a clipped surrogate objective

ℒPPO(θ)=𝔼x∼𝒟,y∼πθold[−∑t=1|y|min(rt(θ)A^t,clip(rt(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)A^t)]\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{PPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D},y\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\left[-\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\min\left(r_{t}(\theta)\hat{A}_{t},\mathrm{clip}(r_{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{t}\right)\right] (1)

where rt​(θ)=πθ​(at|st)πθold​(at|st)r_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{t}|s_{t})}, A^t\hat{A}_{t} is the advantage estimation at step tt, and ϵ\epsilon is a small hyperparameter. Variants of PPO differ in how A^t\hat{A}_{t} is computed. Vanilla PPO estimates token-level advantages via GAE (Schulman et al., 2015):

A^t=∑k=0T−t−1(γ​λ)k​(rt+k+γ​vϕ​(st+k+1)−vϕ​(st+k))\displaystyle\hat{A}_{t}=\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}(\gamma\lambda)^{k}(r_{t+k}+\gamma v_{\phi}(s_{t+k+1})-v_{\phi}(s_{t+k})) (2)

where vϕv_{\phi} is a learned critic model, rtr_{t} is the observed reward at step tt, γ\gamma is the discount factor, and λ\lambda is a hyperparameter. The critic model is trained to minimize MSE towards TD(λ\lambda) targets on the same data distribution. GRPO and RLOO estimate trajectory-level advantages utilizing the rewards of all responses for the same prompt. 4 Limitations of Discriminative Critics

We investigate the limitations of standard discriminative critics in LLM RL from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Our analysis suggests that the difficulty of value learning is not purely an optimization problem, but is also rooted in the limited expressiveness of the one-shot scalar prediction paradigm. These findings motivate the more expressive generative critic developed in the next section.

Theoretical Explanation via Representation Complexity. We study the limitations of standard discriminative critics through the lens of representation complexity. The key issue is not only that value prediction can be noisy or difficult to optimize, but also that the value function itself may be intrinsically difficult to represent with a one-shot scalar predictor. A standard discriminative critic maps a prompt together with a partial response directly to a scalar value in a single forward pass of fixed depth. This raises a natural question: even under stable optimization, is such a predictor expressive enough for value functions arising in sparse-reward language-generation MDPs? Recent theory suggests that the answer can be no. In particular, (Feng and Zhong, 2024) construct a family of MDPs parameterized by an underlying language L∈𝖯L\in\mathsf{P}, and show that the associated value-function computation can already be 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete. This is not a single pathological example, but a fairly general construction template indexed by the underlying language. Meanwhile, log-precision Transformers with constant depth and polynomial hidden dimension are confined to the complexity class 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0} (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2023), which is widely believed to be strictly weaker than 𝖯\mathsf{P}. The implication is that value functions can be substantially harder to represent than a standard scalar critic can express. From this perspective, the difficulty of value learning may stem not only from optimization, but also from a mismatch between the target value function and the expressive capacity of one-shot scalar prediction. Notably, since log-precision Transformers of any practical scale remain within 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0}, this perspective predicts that increasing model size alone, without adding sequential computation, should yield limited improvement, a prediction we test empirically below.11 1 For readers less familiar with the complexity notation, Appendix A provides a short intuition.

Empirical Approximation Performance. To probe this representation-complexity perspective empirically, we isolate value estimation from the rest of RL and fit a fixed value function, namely that of the initial policy Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025). Analogous to the value pretraining stage in (Yuan et al., 2025b), we freeze the actor and train the critic on a held-out split of the DeepScaleR (Luo et al., 2025) prompt dataset. All critics are initialized directly from the Qwen3 base series. Following (Yuan et al., 2025b), we formulate the MDP at the token level and fit Monte Carlo returns. We evaluate on a curated benchmark of state-value pairs, where each state consists of a validation prompt together with a partial response generated by the initial policy and truncated at semantic boundaries. Following (Wang et al., 2024), we estimate the ground-truth value of each state by averaging the final rewards over multiple continuations, and report the mean squared error between these labels and the critic predictions. To study scaling behavior, we train critics across model sizes ranging from 0.60.6B to 1414B. For each size, we tune the learning rate and the amount of training data to obtain stable convergence. We repeat each setup 10 times with different random seeds and report the mean and standard deviation of the final validation MSE in Figure 2(a).

  • •

    Not scalable. Despite substantial increases in pretrained model capacity and training compute, critics across all evaluated sizes achieve remarkably similar approximation errors. This suggests that larger discriminative critics still fail to realize materially better value representations.

  • •

    Not robust. Final performance varies sharply across random seeds for every model size. Since LLMs are typically much less sensitive to such randomness, this variation points to pronounced instability in discriminative value approximation.

Together, these results suggest that discriminative critics face a fundamental expressiveness barrier that cannot be overcome by simply scaling model size. This motivates replacing one-shot scalar prediction with a critic architecture that supports intermediate reasoning, as we develop in the next section.

5 Generative Actor-Critic

The representation-complexity perspective developed in Section 4 clarifies why value modeling may require a more expressive critic parameterization. The appeal of a generative critic is not simply that it produces text before a scalar value, but that it preserves autoregressive generation and thereby enables intermediate reasoning before the final value estimate is produced. Recent work further suggests that such intermediate generation can strictly expand transformer expressive power relative to one-shot prediction (Feng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024). If value modeling is fundamentally constrained by representation complexity, then this additional reasoning channel provides exactly the kind of computation that a critic should exploit.

5.1 Generative Critic

We now describe two core components of our generative critic: a) an autoregressive architecture that enables chain-of-thought reasoning before value estimation, and b) an in-context mechanism for explicit policy conditioning. Together, they form the foundation for the training pipeline in Section 5.2.

Architecture. Standard discriminative critics replace the pretrained language modeling head with a linear projection layer that maps the final hidden states directly to a scalar value prediction. In contrast, our proposed generative critic retains the original language modeling head, fully leveraging pretrained knowledge and allowing the critic to perform explicit chain-of-thought reasoning before arriving at a final value estimate. Instead of prompting the model to verbalize an arbitrary real-valued scalar, we ask the critic to produce an integer score from 00 to 1010 representing the likelihood of success, which we parse and normalize into a value prediction between 00 and 11. This scoring format is inherently more natural for a language model to reason over and predict. We illustrate the advantage estimation computation of value-free methods, discriminative critics, and generative critics in Figure 1.

In-Context Conditioning (ICC). A fundamental distinction between reward functions and value functions is that the latter are conditioned on policies, suggesting that critics must be aware of the specific capabilities of the active policy. Discriminative critics encode all relevant information in their weights, while generative critics, as LLMs with in-context learning capabilities, could additionally exploit explicit policy descriptors provided in context. To this end, we design a prompt template that a) explicitly prompts the critic to infer the actor’s capabilities from the partial response, and b) provides additional information about the actor policy, including its model size and a smoothed running average of the success rate in the training set, as shown in Figure 3. ICC grounds the critic’s reasoning, making a general function approximator more tightly policy-conditioned without requiring it to encode all policy-specific information in weights alone. This is particularly important because, as we show in Section 6.3.1, even a strong LLM such as GPT-5 fails to serve as an accurate value model without sufficient knowledge of the actor. This limitation also applies during joint training, where only a small sample of actor traces is available for critic learning at each iteration. Our ablation confirms that ICC yields consistent improvements across all training stages, validating that in-context policy conditioning is complementary to learned weight adaptation.

5.2 Training Pipeline

Prior to the main RL loop, the generative critic undergoes a two-stage pretraining process: (1) Supervised Finetuning (SFT), which instills foundational reasoning patterns using synthesized reasoning traces, and (2) RL Pretraining, which grounds the critic’s reasoning in empirical, ground-truth returns. Following these stages, the critic is fully initialized and ready for joint-training with the actor.

SFT. To instill the reasoning capabilities into the generative critic, we construct a dataset of high-quality reasoning traces for cold-start SFT. Using a held-out split of the prompt dataset, we sample partial responses generated by the initial actor, apply the critic prompt template in Figure 3, and query GPT-5 (Singh et al., 2025) to generate reasoning traces. We collect these traces and perform standard SFT on the base model. Notably, despite being a strong language model, GPT-5 serves as a relatively weak value model. The purpose of this stage is solely to equip the critic with a functional format and basic value-centric reasoning, rather than distilling value modeling skills from the oracle.

RL Pretraining. While SFT successfully instills reasoning capabilities, the resulting critic struggles to produce accurate value estimates due to two reasons. First, SFT models tend to overfit to stylistic patterns in the data and generalize poorly to unseen states (Tajwar et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2025). Second, the critic’s performance is inherently upper-bounded by the oracle, which cannot perfectly simulate the initial policy’s true performance due to insufficient in-context information (details in Section 6.3.1). To bridge this gap, we freeze the actor and train the critic via RL, directly grounding its reasoning in empirical returns. Specifically, we train the critic using REINFORCE Williams (1992) to optimize a rule-based reward. For each state ss, the critic generates a reasoning trace zz yielding a parsed value prediction v^\hat{v}, which is evaluated against the observed reward rr: Rv​(s,z)=1−(r−v^)2R_{v}(s,z)=1-(r-\hat{v})^{2}. If parsing v^\hat{v} from zz fails, we set the reward to 00. This reward is motivated by the MSE minimization objective used to train discriminative critics in standard PPO, while additionally enforcing valid output format. Following (Yuan et al., 2025b), we set GAE λ=1\lambda=1 and remove the KL penalty. Training stops when validation MSE saturates.

RL Joint-Training. Once pretrained, the generative critic is integrated into the downstream RL loop. The procedure is identical to RL pretraining, except that the actor is now updated via PPO using advantages computed from the critic’s predictions. By alternating between actor and critic updates, the critic continuously adapts its reasoning to track the shifting value function of the evolving actor, so that credit assignment remains accurate as the policy evolves. A detailed pseudo code is provided in Appendix B.

Cost Analysis. We conduct a cost analysis in Appendix C. Compared to standard PPO, GenAC incurs approximately 2.1×2.1\times the computational cost per iteration. However, as we show in Section 6.2, this overhead is offset by improved sample efficiency and continued performance gains in regimes where a discriminative critic saturates. In this work, we prioritize demonstrating the performance gains achievable through stronger value modeling, and leave engineering optimizations for reducing computational overhead to future work.

6 Experiments

6.1 Approximation Performance

We repeat the controlled approximation experiment from Section 4, now training generative critics under the same protocol. As shown in Figure 2(a), generative critics achieve substantially lower approximation error than their discriminative counterparts at every model size. Moreover, their error decreases consistently as model size increases and exhibits markedly lower variance across random seeds, addressing both failure modes identified in Section 4.

6.2 RL Experiment

We now present our primary evaluation, conducting extensive RL training experiments on mathematical reasoning to assess the effectiveness of our method.

Setup. We adopt a zero RL setup (Guo et al., 2025a), initializing the policy with Qwen3-8B-Base (Yang et al., 2025) and the critic with our pretrained generative critic as detailed in Section 5. Models are trained on the DeepScaleR dataset (Luo et al., 2025) and evaluated across six standard mathematical reasoning benchmarks: AIME 2024, AMC 2023, MATH 500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), AIME 2025, OlympiadBench (He et al., 2024), and Minerva Math (Lewkowycz et al., 2022). For all evaluations, we report the average accuracy over 16 sampled generations per problem.

Baselines. We compare GenAC against three RL baselines: GRPO, RLOO, and VC-PPO. As PPO variants, all algorithms share the same underlying policy optimization framework and differ solely in their advantage estimation mechanisms. GRPO and RLOO serve as value-free baselines that estimate advantages using sample scores, while VC-PPO leverages a pretrained discriminative critic.

Performance of GenAC. From Figure 2(b) and Table 1, our proposed GenAC achieves the strongest overall and final performance. Notably, it is significantly more sample-efficient, requiring fewer training steps to outperform baselines. Furthermore, its performance margin over all baselines continues to grow as training progresses. We attribute this success to the generative value function that provides fine-grained feedback compared to bandit-style baselines, and enables more accurate credit assignment than standard discriminative critic in VC-PPO.

The Role of Value Modeling. Our comparison of advantage estimators reveals a clear hierarchy in policy performance: GenAC outperforms VC-PPO, which in turn outperforms the bandit-style baselines. Benefiting from fine-grained feedback, both GenAC and VC-PPO are more sample-efficient than GRPO or RLOO during the early stages of training. However, constrained by the representational limits of its discriminative critic, VC-PPO’s advantage diminishes over time, ultimately resulting in a policy only marginally above the value-free baselines. In contrast, leveraging a more expressive generative critic, GenAC sustains this momentum and achieves an increasing performance margin. These observations strongly suggest that improvements in value modeling directly translate to superior policy performance in LLM RL, demonstrating that explicit, accurate value modeling remains a critical driver for effective and efficient policy optimization.

6.3 Analysis

Having established the RL training performance, we now take a closer look at the generative critic itself, probing its design choices and characteristic properties through a series of targeted analyses.

6.3.1 Ablation Studies

To disentangle the contributions of the training stages and the ICC mechanism, we conduct an ablation study evaluating value function approximation performance and summarize the results in Table 3.

The Challenge of Zero-Shot Value Estimation. A critical observation is that even GPT-5, the oracle model we use to synthesize SFT data, struggles to serve as an accurate value function via prompting alone. This stands in sharp contrast to the success of LLM-as-a-Judge in reward modeling. We attribute this discrepancy to the fundamental requirement of policy-conditioning. Without explicit training, even a strong generalist model fails to accurately predict the value of a specific policy, highlighting the necessity of our specialized training pipeline.

Impact of Training Stages. While SFT provides a massive improvement over the base model by distilling the necessary reasoning capabilities, its performance is bounded by the limited quality of supervision. RL pretraining is therefore necessary, as it enables continuous improvement by optimizing directly towards observed rewards.

Efficacy of ICC. We observe that removing ICC consistently degrades performance across all configurations. Although ICC alone is insufficient to transform a generalist LLM into an accurate value model, this consistent benefit indicates that it provides additional information that the model weights alone cannot fully capture, effectively enhancing the precision of value estimation.

6.3.2 Relative Ranking Performance

While approximation error measures the absolute performance of value models, RL optimization depends heavily on relative comparisons due to mechanisms like advantage estimation and group sampling. Therefore, assessing value prediction quality requires a relative ranking probe.

Setup. To evaluate this capability, we generate multiple candidate segments per prompt, compute their ground truth values using the average score of Monte Carlo rollouts, and score them with either discriminative or generative critic. We measure the top-1 accuracy, i.e. the ratio of prompts where the critic’s highest-scoring candidate matches the candidate with the highest ground truth value, and report the results in Table 3.

Results. The results demonstrate that the generative critic consistently outperforms its discriminative counterpart across all candidate pool sizes. Crucially, the performance gap widens as the decision space grows larger: the discriminative critic’s accuracy degrades quickly towards random chance while the generative critic maintains a much higher accuracy. This indicates that in addition to yielding better absolute approximation, the generative critic provides a more reliable advantage signal for distinguishing between possible actions.

6.3.3 Generalization

Although value models are mostly responsible for providing accurate feedback on in-distribution (ID) training data, their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization is crucial for effective and stable learning on exploratory off-policy data. A critic that overfits superficial ID patterns will provide noisy or degenerate feedback that hinders the learning process and could lead to premature convergence.

Setup. To assess this robustness, we apply our approximation performance evaluation to the pretrained critics across a spectrum of datasets with increasing degrees of distributional shift. Concretely, we progressively move from exact ID training (DeepScaleR) to mathematical problems of varying difficulty (Math500 for easier and AIME24 for harder), and finally to a distinct domain of general scientific reasoning (GPQA (Rein et al., 2024)).

Results. The evaluation in Table 4 reveals that the two architectures differ markedly in generalization. While the generative critic achieves a modest MSE reduction on in-distribution data compared to the discriminative baseline, its relative advantage increases significantly as the distributional shift grows, reaching over 50% reduction on AIME24. This suggests that the generative critic evaluates reasoning quality based on transferable patterns rather than distribution-specific memorization. This stronger generalization helps explain the growing performance gap between GenAC and VC-PPO in Figure 2(b): as the actor policy evolves away from its initialization, the generative critic continues to provide reliable feedback while the discriminative critic degrades.

6.3.4 Case Study

We present a qualitative case study in Figure 4. The problem asks for the xx-coordinate where two curves have parallel tangents. After a correct prefix (Steps 1–3) that differentiates both curves and equates derivatives, the critic recognizes this sound progress and assigns a value of 0.60.6. In Step 4, the actor commits a conceptual error by requiring parallel tangents to share the same yy-value, dismissing a valid solution. The critic precisely identifies this misconception, arguing that parallel tangents require only equal slopes, and assigns a low value of 0.10.1. Notably, as these predictions are independent, the sharp value drop emerges from two accurate assessments. This example illustrates that the generative critic is able to assign credit accurately and interpretably.

7 Conclusion and Future Work

This work re-establishes learned value models as a critical driver of effective LLM post-training by identifying a key source of their historical instability as a representational limitation of discriminative architectures, and addressing it through a generative critic equipped with chain-of-thought reasoning and In-Context Conditioning. As early work on raising the performance ceiling of RL through better value modeling, we primarily focus on demonstrating what becomes possible with accurate credit assignment, leaving engineering efforts toward reducing computational cost to future work. While our experiments are conducted on mathematical reasoning tasks, the benefits of accurate value modeling are expected to generalize broadly. As LLM post-training continues to push into longer horizon and more complex settings such as agentic systems, credit assignment will only grow more critical, and we believe expressive value modeling is a natural and necessary foundation for continued progress.

Appendix A Background on Representation Complexity

Complexity Classes 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0} and 𝖯\mathsf{P}. The complexity class 𝖯\mathsf{P} denotes problems solvable in polynomial time, which may still require many sequential computational steps. In contrast, 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0} denotes computations realizable by polynomial-size, constant-depth threshold circuits, which are far more parallel and far less sequential. In particular, prior work shows that log-precision Transformers with constant depth and polynomial hidden dimension are confined to the complexity class 𝖳𝖢0\mathsf{TC}^{0} [40]. The widely held assumption 𝖳𝖢0≠𝖯\mathsf{TC}^{0}\neq\mathsf{P} therefore says that some polynomial-time computations cannot be compressed into a constant number of layers.

Value-Focused Restatement from [39]. A value-focused restatement of their result is as follows. They construct a family of 𝖯\mathsf{P} MDPs indexed by an underlying language L∈𝖯L\in\mathsf{P}, so the result applies to a broad class of constructions rather than a single bespoke example. When LL is 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete, computing the optimal value function for the corresponding MDP family is itself 𝖯\mathsf{P}-complete. In other words, even for an explicitly specified finite MDP, evaluating the correct value at a state can already capture the full difficulty of arbitrary polynomial-time computation. Their expressiveness result makes the implication for standard neural predictors more concrete: under the assumption 𝖳𝖢0≠𝖯\mathsf{TC}^{0}\neq\mathsf{P}, these value functions cannot be represented by constant-depth, polynomial-width MLPs or Transformers. The takeaway is that value computation may intrinsically require more sequential reasoning than a shallow one-shot predictor can express.

Appendix B Implementation Details

Pseudo Code. The pseudo code for GenAC joint training is presented in Algorithm 1. In line 13, the actor’s response is segmented into a sequence of short segments using heuristic delimiter-based rules. In line 20, the resulting segment-level value predictions are broadcast back to token-level to match the token-level objective in standard PPO. In line 21, we use GAE with λ=1\lambda=1, which reduces the advantage estimate to r−vr-v.

Code. We develop our code based on verl [53] with vLLM [54] engine and FSDP [55] backend. All experiments are conducted on a node of Nvidia 80G A100 GPUs.

Hyperparameters. All hyperparameters are detailed in Table 5, largely following the example scripts in verl.

Approximation Experiment Details. For discriminative critics, we perform a hyperparameter search over learning rates in {1​e−5,5​e−6,4​e−6,2​e−6,1​e−6}\{1e-5,5e-6,4e-6,2e-6,1e-6\} and training steps in {100,200}\{100,200\} per model size. For generative critics, we fix the learning rate to 1​e−61e-6 and the number of training steps to 100100, as they are much more robust to such variation. See Table 6 for the final selected hyperparameters.

Appendix C Computational Cost Analysis of GenAC

We analyze the total computational cost of GenAC in comparison to PPO and VinePPO, two baselines with fine-grained feedback. Following standard practice, we decompose FLOPs into three components:

Cgeneration\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{generation}} =2​P​T\displaystyle=2PT
Cforward\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{forward}} =2​P​T\displaystyle=2PT
Ctrain\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{train}} =6​P​T\displaystyle=6PT

where PP is the number of model parameters and TT is the total number of tokens processed.

PPO. PPO involves a discriminative critic of similar size to the actor.

CPPO\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{PPO}} =2​Pa​T\displaystyle=2P_{a}T (actor generation)
+2​Pa​T\displaystyle+2P_{a}T (actor forward)
+6​Pa​T\displaystyle+6P_{a}T (actor train)
+2​Pc​T\displaystyle+2P_{c}T (critic forward)
+6​Pc​T\displaystyle+6P_{c}T (critic train)
=10​Pa​T+8​Pc​T≈18​P​T.\displaystyle=10P_{a}T+8P_{c}T\approx 18PT.

GenAC. GenAC utilizes a generative critic, generating and learning on different tokens. Let L1L_{1} denote the average segment length and L2L_{2} the average critic generation length. The total tokens processed by the critic are

Tc=T+TL1⋅L2,\displaystyle T_{c}=T+\frac{T}{L_{1}}\cdot L_{2},

where the first term accounts for the longest actor prefix and the second for the tokens it generates. With L1≈120L_{1}\approx 120 and L2≈300L_{2}\approx 300, we obtain Tc≈3.5​TT_{c}\approx 3.5T, giving

CGenAC\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{GenAC}} =2​Pa​T\displaystyle=2P_{a}T (actor generation)
+2​Pa​T\displaystyle+2P_{a}T (actor forward)
+6​Pa​T\displaystyle+6P_{a}T (actor train)
+2​Pc​Tc\displaystyle+2P_{c}T_{c} (critic generation)
+6​Pc​Tc\displaystyle+6P_{c}T_{c} (critic train)
=10​Pa​T+8​Pc​Tc≈38​P​T.\displaystyle=10P_{a}T+8P_{c}T_{c}\approx 38PT.

VinePPO. VinePPO estimates values via branched Monte Carlo rollouts. Let L2′L_{2}^{\prime} denote the average branched-rollout length and nn the number of branches per prefix. The total branching tokens are

Tr=TL1⋅L2′⋅n\displaystyle T_{r}=\frac{T}{L_{1}}\cdot L_{2}^{\prime}\cdot n

With L1≈120L_{1}\approx 120, L2′≈1024L_{2}^{\prime}\approx 1024, and n=4n=4, we have Tr≈34​TT_{r}\approx 34T, giving

CVinePPO\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{VinePPO}} =2​P​T\displaystyle=2PT (actor generation)
+2​P​T\displaystyle+2PT (actor forward)
+6​P​T\displaystyle+6PT (actor train)
+2​P​Tr\displaystyle+2PT_{r} (branched rollouts)
≈78​P​T.\displaystyle\approx 78PT.

Summary. Table 7 summarizes the relative costs. At 2.1×2.1\times the FLOPs of PPO, GenAC’s overhead compares favorably with VinePPO’s 4.3×4.3\times. More importantly, the overhead reflects a qualitative gain, as GenAC steadily improves with more samples while PPO saturates early. Our primary focus is raising the ceiling of RL through better value modeling; engineering efforts to reduce training cost are left to future work.
